newsitem.title: USA: Pan Am return dismays Lockerbie victims' relatives.
newsitem.headline: Pan Am return dismays Lockerbie victims' relatives.

text.p: An organisation of relatives of people killed in the 1988 Lockerbie airliner bombing reacted with dismay to the news that Pan Am would be flying again next week, saying they were concerned about its management.
The airline collapsed in debt in 1991, weakened by stiff industry competition and by the bombing of Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, in which 270 people were killed.
It will take to the skies again on Sept. 26.
"We are really greatly saddened because we feel it is a disservice to the flying public," Victoria Cummock, president of the Families of Pan Am 103/Lockerbie, said.
She said the group had no objection to the name Pan Am itself returning, but "we are very concerned about who's running it".
The Department of Transportation gave its clearance on Wednesday for the new Pan Am to begin operations, dismissing a petition from the Families group.
The first flight will take off from Miami for New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport next Thursday with another flight from New York to Los Angeles, spokesman Jeff Kriendler said.

Florida businessmen Chuck Cobb and Martin Shugrue bought the Pan Am name and logo in 1993 with the plan of eventually resurrecting the carrier, which had been one of the commercial aviation industry's pioneers. A number of the old managers have been brought in.
The new Pan Am hopes to benefit from the illustrious name. But Kriendler conceded that the company was also taking onboard a certain stigma from the bombing.
"Certainly there is the association," he said. "But most people have fond memories of Pan Am over the years and hopefully they will not be influenced by this tragedy."
